The Taraba State Government has approved the payment of outstanding allowances and other entitlements to workers in state-owned tertiary institutions.
Governor Agbu Kefas said the approval covers the Consolidated Academic Teaching Allowance (CATA), Consolidated Non-Teaching Tools Allowance (CONTTA), Earned Academic Allowance (EAA) and other related entitlements.
The governor announced the decision in a statement posted on his verified X account on Wednesday.
He said it followed the recommendations of a committee set up to examine the workers’ demands after months of negotiations involving the government, the Joint Action Committee of Tertiary Institutions in Taraba State (JACTI), the Academic Staff Union of Universities (ASUU), Taraba State University chapter, and other unions.
Mr Kefas appealed to the striking unions and workers to suspend their industrial actions to allow academic activities to resume across the affected institutions.
“Our students have suffered enough. These strikes have disrupted examinations and caused avoidable hardship that no child should have to endure,” he said.
He added that the government would continue engaging with the unions to address outstanding concerns within available resources.

The approval comes after weeks of industrial action by workers in the state’s tertiary institutions over unpaid allowances and other employment-related grievances.
On 6 November, JACTI declared a two-week warning strike, accusing the state government of failing to address its demands despite the expiration of a 14-day strike ultimatum.
The committee, which represents workers in five state-owned tertiary institutions, said the decision followed more than four months of unsuccessful negotiations over the implementation of CATA, CONTTA and EAA.
In a statement issued after a meeting in Jalingo on 5 November, JACTI Chairman Misa Gaji and Secretary Abdulkarim Dangana listed other grievances, including salary deductions for identity cards and APER forms without the items being issued, and deductions for health insurance without enrolment.
They also complained about the non-implementation of annual increments and step movements for more than 10 years, withheld union dues and multipurpose savings, and the non-payment of the N70,000 transport relief for public servants.
The committee said the government’s silence had frustrated efforts to resolve the dispute and warned that failure to address the demands after the warning strike could lead to indefinite industrial action.
The latest intervention follows Mr Kefas’s visit to Taraba State University, Jalingo, on 29 October, when he appealed to striking lecturers to return to work in the interest of students and the institution’s academic calendar.
During the visit, the governor announced the formation of a committee to examine the lecturers’ demands and review the existing salary and allowance structure.
He also said the government would work towards a uniform and sustainable salary system for the state’s tertiary institutions.
Mr Kefas expressed optimism that approval of the committee’s recommendations would lead to the immediate resumption of academic activities across the affected institutions.
However, he did not specify when the approved allowances would be paid or whether the unions had agreed to suspend their industrial actions.
